newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso sees re-election plan advance.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso sees re-election plan advance.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's plan to seek an unprecedented second term in 1998 moved forward on Wednesday when a congressional committee approved a bill allowing re-election.

The bill, considered the biggest challenge for Cardoso in seeking another term, must now be approved in the full Chamber of Deputies, where the government's fragile multiparty alliance has been undermined by opposition to re-election.
"I am sure that from now on re-election will take on a new lease of life," Benito Gama, the government's chief whip in the lower house, said.
The chances of its winning on the floor of the lower house depend on the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), the largest party in Congress, which is split on the issue.
"We hope to sit down with the PMDB today and see if we can vote next week," a government official said. "Half the PMDB is open to negotiation, half isn't."

But a government-allied lawmaker was less optimistic about the government's chances of persuading the PMDB to vote. "It would take a miracle. The PMDB can't go into a vote like this with the party in pieces," the deputy said.

The PMDB, which generally supports Cardoso and has four ministers in his cabinet, stunned the government on Sunday when a party convention dominated by its anti-government wing recommended members abstain from voting on re-election until Feb. 15, after internal elections in Congress.

With Congress in turmoil, the government was forced to postpone a vote by the lower house panel set for Tuesday. The PMDB's six members of the panel eventually agreed to vote on Wednesday but only after Cardoso appealed for action.
Cardoso has hinted he might call a plebicite to settle the issue if Congress continued to drag its heels, but officials said a national vote on re-election was a last resort.
"The plebicite might be considered if there's no chance of re-election advancing in Congress," Jose Anibal, a whip with Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party, said.
Cardoso is seeking to become Brazil's first re-elected president since the founding of the republic in 1889 by rewriting the constitution and running in the 1998 presidential elections.
